title: Almost every gene set reads higher in the index arm: a size-matched empirical null for small rare-tumour expression series, and what it leaves of the EWSR1::NR4A3 direct-target catalogue
abstract: Small studies of rare cancers can make many unrelated groups of genes appear unusually active. We asked whether genes proposed to be controlled by NR4A3 fusion proteins, made when NR4A3 is joined to another gene, in extraskeletal myxoid chondrosarcoma (EMC) stood out from that background. We compared the proposed group with randomly chosen groups of the same size, separately on each measurement platform. Our literature search identified three genes with assays showing an NR4A3 fusion binding DNA. Three was too few for the scoring method, so we grouped them with sixteen targets of the normal NR4A3 protein. This distinction matters: the combined group is not a set of nineteen demonstrated fusion targets. The combined group did not exceed the random-group threshold on either of the two usable expression-array platforms. A previously published EMC expression signature exceeded both thresholds. Among the three genes, SEMA3C changed direction with the comparison tumors. PPARG's strongest result reused the dataset in which it was discovered. ENO3 remained elevated across the expression checks, but it had been selected beforehand as a gene expected to test positive, so this is not an independent discovery. Our bounded search found no measurements of NR4A3-fusion DNA binding in EMC material. Available binding measurements concern other proteins or tissues; two apparently positive comparisons did not survive correction for the number of comparisons. The cohorts are small and their comparison groups differ. These findings show why an attractive expression pattern needs a background comparison. They do not establish which genes the fusion causes to change. Binding and controlled fusion-perturbation experiments in EMC are needed to address that question.
